walkthroughs.body_html:
Weight is a force. W = m × g.

On Earth, g ≈ 10 N/kg. So a 5 kg cat weighs 5 × 10 = 50 N. 🐱

On the Moon, g is only about 1.6 N/kg. Same cat, much less weight — but the same mass!

If a resultant force acts on a mass, it accelerates. F = m × a.

A 6 kg trolley with a resultant force of 18 N accelerates at 18 ÷ 6 = 3 m/s².

Bigger mass needs bigger force for the same acceleration. Heavy things are stubborn.

When a force moves something, it does work: W = F × d.

Push a box with 20 N for 3 m and you've done 60 J of work. The unit of work is the joule (J).

No movement = no work done, even if you're sweating holding a heavy bag. 💪

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
Mass changes with location but weight does not.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: Mass changes with location but weight does not.
Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the gravitational force on that mass (N) and depends on g.
Mass and weight are the same thing, just expressed in different units.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.

mcqs.q: If air resistance is ignored, which falls faster: a heavy ball or a light ball dropped from the same height?
options: Mass changes with location but weight does not.
Both fall at the same rate because gravitational acceleration is independent of mass.
Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects because gravity pulls more on them.
The lighter ball falls faster because it has less inertia.
